Court of King’s Bench of Alberta

Citation: R v Borhot, ABKB 2025 696

Date:
20251201

Docket:
220970341Q1

Registry:
Calgary

Between:

His Majesty the King

Crown

Jamal Taan Borhot

Defendant

Notice

By Court Order: All materials filed in the context of this application are subject to the Restricted Access Application and some materials are subject to a Sealing Order. This decision has been approved for release to the public.

_______________________________________________________

Reasons for Decision

of the

Honourable Justice

C. Dario

_______________________________________________________

I.

INTRODUCTION

[
1
]

Jamal Taan Borhot (Accused) is charged with three terrorism offences contrary to s 83.18 of the
Criminal Code of Canada
, RSC 1985, c C-46 (
Criminal Code
). The alleged offences occurred between May 9, 2013 and April 8, 2014 in Syria. The Accused is alleged to have left Canada and entered and remained in Syria for the purposes of participating in or contributing to the activities of a terrorist group.

[
2
]

The Crown alleges the Accused left Canada and entered Syria illegally via Kilis, Turkey with the intention of joining a terrorist group. Once inside Syria, the Accused engaged in training and other activities for the benefit of the Islamic State. During the 11 months the Accused was in Syria, he is alleged to have either joined the Islamic State, or Jabhat al-Nusra/al-Nusra Front (al Nusra) and then the Islamic State for whom he engaged in fighting, administrative duties, and leadership duties. He is alleged to have attempted to recruit others to join him in fighting in Syria for the benefit of the group with whom he was aligned. After being imprisoned by the Islamic State for stealing medications, the Accused decided to leave Syria. He made his way to Istanbul, applied for and received an emergency passport, and returned to Canada on April 19, 2014.

[
3
]

The Defence offers no specific defence but argues the Crown has not proved beyond a reasonable doubt the essential elements of the offences.

II.

THE CHARGES

[
4
]

The Accused stands charged:

COUNT 1: That between the 9th day of May, 2013 and the 8th day of April 2014, in Syria and elsewhere, did knowingly participate in or contribute to, directly or indirectly, the activities of a terrorist group, by leaving Canada, or by entering Syria, for the benefit of, at the direction of or in association with the terrorist group for the purpose of enhancing the ability of the terrorist group to facilitate or carry out a terrorist activity contrary to
Criminal Code

s 83.18(1).

COUNT 2: That between the 9th day of May, 2013 and the 8th day of April 2014, in Syria and elsewhere, did knowingly participate in or contribute to, directly or indirectly, the activities of a terrorist group, to wit: the Islamic State, by remaining in Syria for the benefit of, at the direction of or in association with the terrorist group for the purpose of enhancing the ability of the terrorist group to facilitate or carry out a terrorist activity contrary to
Criminal Code

s 83.18(1).

COUNT 3: That between the 9th day of May, 2013 and the 8th day of April 2014, in Syria and elsewhere, did knowingly participate in or contribute to, directly or indirectly, the activities of a terrorist group, to wit: the Islamic State, by committing acts, including one or more terrorist activities for the purpose of enhancing the ability of the terrorist group to facilitate or carry out a terrorist activity, contrary to
Criminal Code

s 83.18(1).

[
5
]

In addition to the particulars of each charge the Crown must prove beyond a reasonable doubt that:

(a)

A terrorist group existed;

(b)

The Accused knew of the existence of that terrorist group;

(c)

The Accused participated in, or contributed to, directly or indirectly, any activity of that terrorist group; and

(d)

The Accused’s participation or contribution was intended by the Accused to enhance the ability of a terrorist group to facilitate or carry out a terrorist activity.

[
6
]

With respect to Count 1, the Crown must also prove the Accused left Canada or entered Syria for the benefit of, at the direction of, or in association with at least one terrorist group. The terrorist group is not particularized. With respect to Count 2, the Crown must also prove the Accused remained in Syria for the benefit of, at the direction of, or in association with the Islamic State. With respect to Count 3, the Crown must also prove the Accused committed acts, including one or more terrorist activities for the benefit of, at the direction of, or in association with the Islamic State.

III.

UNDISPUTED FACTS

[
7
]

At the outset of the trial, the Defence made no admissions and put the Crown to the strict proof of their case. However, the Defence did not dispute some facts alleged by the Crown.

[
8
]

The Defence does not admit the Accused left Canada and travelled to Syria. However, the Defence does not dispute the following:

•

The Accused was absent from Calgary (his city of residence), from May 9, 2013 to April 19, 2014;

•

The Accused arrived at the Calgary International Airport on April 19, 2014, from an international flight;

•

On April 19, 2014 the Accused was detained at the Calgary International Airport by Canadian Border Services Agency and interviewed by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) during that detention; and

•

The Accused participated in three recorded interviews with the RCMP on April 19, 2014, May 22, 2014, and May 18, 2020;

•

The content of the Accused`s three recorded RCMP interviews.

[
9
]

The Defence does not dispute the Accused has a Facebook account. However, the Defence does not admit the Accused’s Facebook account is the one containing the posts and messages tendered by the Crown or that the Accused authored any of those posts or messages.

[
10
]

The Defence does not dispute the Accused has a cousin named Hussein Borhot (Hussein), his mother is Zeinab Borhot (Zeinab), or he lived with Zeinab in Calgary at 2020 Pinetree Cresc (Pinetree) before he left Calgary on May 9, 2014 and after he returned to Calgary on April 19, 2014.

[
11
]

The Defence does not dispute the RCMP embarked on an investigation into the activities of the Accused and Hussein, or the investigation was named “Project Saddle II” by the RCMP.

[
12
]

The Defence does not dispute the RCMP engaged in surveillance and installed wiretaps to investigate the Accused’s activities. However, the Defence does not admit the Accused participated in any of the recorded conversations or was the person the RCMP identified as the Accused in those recorded conversations.

[
13
]

With respect to world events during the 11 months the Accused was away from Calgary, the Defence does not dispute a civil war against the government led by Bashar al-Assad (al-Assad Regime) was raging in Syria. Nor does the Defence dispute that al-Qaeda, al Nusra, and the Islamic State were active in Syria during that time or that those three entities are terrorist organizations and listed as such by the Government of Canada. However, the Defence does dispute whether they were terrorist organizations or the Accused knew or should have known they were terrorist organizations at the time he is alleged to have travelled to and/or been in Syria.

[
14
]

With respect to listed terrorist groups, the Defence does not dispute the following:

•

The Islamic State was listed as a terrorist organization by Canada as early as 2006;

•

The United States declared al Nusra to be a terrorist organization in 2012;

•

Canada listed al Nusra as a terrorist organization in November 2013;

•

The Islamic State in Syria and the Levant, and the Islamic State in Syria and Iraq were not listed as terrorist organizations in Canada until September 2014;

•

The Islamic State declared a Caliphate in Syria in the summer of 2014.

[
15
]

The Defence does not dispute that AK-47 assault rifles were common weapons used in the Syrian civil war.

[
16
]

The Defence acknowledges the accuracy of the Crown expert Dr Steinberg’s evidence regarding the evolution of the Islamic State and its presence in Syria during the relevant time. However, the Defence disputes whether the Islamic State’s agenda would have been apparent to those fighting on the front lines against the al-Assad Regime. The Defence also suggests Dr Steinberg’s evidence was limited to the Islamic State’s involvement in Syria, which excluded consideration of any other group active in opposing the al-Assad Regime.

[
17
]

The Defence acknowledges corroboration is not necessary for a finding of guilt. However, he notes there is no corroboration for the activities alleged to have been committed by the Accused.

[
18
]

The Defence argues the Court must reflect on the nature of the allegations. They are unusual in that they occurred outside of Canada and did not involve any Canadian assets or targets. The Court must be careful not to find liability simply because the Accused was fighting on the “wrong side.” The Court must not assume negative facts merely because the Accused is a young Muslim man with fundamentalist Islamic beliefs.

IV.

RELIABILITY OF THE EVIDENCE

1)

The Law

[
19
]

The Crown’s case is almost entirely circumstantial. Inferences must be drawn from the totality of the evidence and are to be assessed logically, and in light of human experience and common sense. An inference of guilt drawn from circumstantial evidence should be the only reasonable inference the evidence permits:
R v Villaroman
,
2016 SCC 33
[
Villaroman
]

at para
30
.

[
20
]

The reasonable doubt standard must not be applied to individual pieces of evidence:
R v Morin
,
1988 CanLII 8 (SCC)
[
Morin
] at para
33
. Rather, the Court must examine the evidence as a whole to determine whether the only reasonable inference that can be drawn from the circumstantial evidence is the accused’s guilt:
R v Griffin
,
2009 SCC 28
at para
33
;
Morin
at para
40
. Individual pieces of circumstantial evidence are bricks with which to construct a wall. Examined separately and in isolation, individual pieces of evidence may not have a strong probative force. But the pieces of evidence must be considered in relation to the whole. It is the whole of the evidence taken together whose cumulative force must be considered as a basis for a finding of guilt:
R v Maure
,
2024 ABKB 717
[
Maure
] at para
98
; see also
R v Anny
,
2021 ABCA 394
at para
57
, and
R v Okojie
,
2021 ONCA 773
at para
142
.

[
21
]

The Court should consider other reasonable possibilities inconsistent with guilt. If there are reasonable inferences other than guilt, the Crown’s evidence does not meet the standard of proof beyond a reasonable doubt:
Villaroman

at para
35
. Inferences consistent with innocence do not have to arise from proven facts:
R v Khela
,
2009 SCC 4
at para
58
. However, reasonable doubt cannot arise from speculation or conjecture:
Villaroman

at para
50
. Theories alternative to guilt must be reasonable given the evidence or absence of evidence, assessed logically, and in light of human experience and common sense:
Villaroman

at para
36
. They must be more than mere speculation or baseless “what-if” arguments:
Maure

at para
103
. A reasonable doubt or theory alternative to guilt is not rendered speculative by the mere fact that it arises from a lack of evidence:
Villaroman

at para
36
.

[
22
]

While the Crown may need to negate reasonable alternatives to guilt, the Crown does not need to negate every possible conjecture that might be consistent with innocence:
Villaroman

at para
37
. That an accused offers in evidence or argument an explanation consistent with innocence does not necessarily mean there is another reasonable inference consistent with innocence:
R v Cabrera
2019 ABCA 184
at para
168
. If the totality of the evidence makes it unlikely the innocent alternative explanations for each individual piece of evidence could all simultaneously be true, the alternative explanations will not raise a reasonable doubt:
Maure

at para
141
.

[
23
]

An accused’s lack of testimony cannot be used to strengthen the Crown’s case where the Crown has fallen short of proving guilt:
R v Noble
1997 CanLII 388 (SCC)
[
Noble
] at para
28
. However, when an accused does not testify, it is open to the trier of fact to draw the inference that they could not have raised a reasonable doubt in the face of convincing Crown evidence:
R v François
,
1994 CanLII 52 (SCC)
at p 835;
Noble

at paras
76-78
. The Court need not speculate about possible defences that might have been offered by an accused had they testified:
Noble

at para
77
. It is helpful to look at the process in two stages: 1) has the Crown adduced evidence which, if believed, would support a conviction? If yes, 2) should the Crown’s evidence be believed? Only during the second stage can the Court consider whether the Crown’s evidence stands unchallenged:
Noble
, McLachlin J in dissent

at paras 119-120. It is not reversing the burden of proof or lightening the Crown’s burden if the Court finds, as a matter of reason and common sense, the evidence that does exist justifies inferences absent evidence to the contrary:
R v deKock
,
2009 ABCA 225 at para 12
.

[
24
]

The circumstantial evidence led in this case includes air tickets, Facebook posts and messages, and wiretap recordings with aids of translations for the Facebook evidence and recordings. It also includes also lay and expert witness evidence, police interviews and transcripts, affidavits, an agreed statement of facts, and the supporting documents for some of this evidence (exhibit reports, MLAT record requests, etc).

2)

Air Travel

[
25
]

I am satisfied the Accused travelled from Calgary to Istanbul, Turkey with Hussein on May 9 and 10, 2013. I am also satisfied neither the Accused nor Hussein travelled from Istanbul, Turkey to Calgary on June 3 and 4, 2013, despite the tickets purchased for those dates.

[
26
]

Exhibit 1 contains records showing on April 16, 2013, Hussein Borhot booked two sets of flights with Flight Network. The flights were booked for two travellers: Hussein Sobhe Borhot (DOB Aug 6, 1985) and Jamal Borhot (DOB March 5, 1990). One reference number was issued for the entire booking. Each traveller was issued a single ticket number for all flights. Those records were obtained by way of a Production Order that sought documents and data specific to the two ticket numbers and the single reference number.

[
27
]

The first set of flights was booked on Air Canada for May 9 and 10, 2013 departing from Calgary and arriving in Istanbul, Turkey by way of Frankfurt, Germany. Reservation records, electronic tickets, and departure control system records were produced in response to the Production Order. Those records all confirm a traveller with the name and birthdate of the Accused boarded both flights.

[
28
]

In interviews with the RCMP on May 22, 2014 and May 18, 2020, the Accused admitted he travelled with his cousin Hussein from Calgary to Istanbul, Turkey on May 9 and 10, 2013. The Defence does not dispute that fact.

[
29
]

The second set of flights was booked on United Airlines for June 3 and 4, 2013 from Istanbul, Turkey to Calgary by way of Newark, New Jersey, United States. No reservation records, electronic tickets, or departure control system records from those flights were produced in response to the Production Order, suggesting the tickets were not used.

3)

Facebook Evidence

[
30
]

The Crown tenders evidence from a Facebook account with the URL www.facebook.com/jamal.borhot1 (Facebook Account) as belonging to the Accused. These include several open-source posts to the Facebook Account’s page (posts) and private direct messages back and forth between the Facebook Account and other Facebook users (messages).

a)

Authentication, Accuracy and Reliability of the Translations

[
31
]

The Crown submits the issues relating to authenticity, continuity, and integrity of the posts and messages was decided in
R v Borhot

2024 ABKB 440
[
Borhot voir dire
]. Likewise decided was the issue of the accuracy and reliability of translations of the posts and messages, including the translations by RCMP civilian translator Rima Hanna (Hanna), and RCMP Cpl Bassam El-Asmar, who speaks Arabic. The Crown submits the truth of the contents of the posts and messages are now evidence to be weighed along with other evidence to determine the issue of the Accused’s innocence or guilt:
R v Evans
,
1993 CanLII 86 (SCC)
[
Evans
] at 668-69.

[
32
]

The Defence submits the reliability threshold for admissibility of the posts and messages is lower and takes into consideration different factors than those to be considered with respect to the ultimate reliability of the posts and messages. As such, all these issues are still to be decided in the trial proper.

[
33
]

I agree the factors to be considered for threshold admissibility and ultimate reliability of this evidence are different. There was compelling evidence supporting admissibility, as described in
Borhot

voir dire
. There has been no evidence tendered in the trial proper suggesting this evidence should be given no weight. For example, there is no evidence suggesting continuity of the posts and messages was compromised. No witness denied the messages were recognizable as messages between the witness and the Accused. Any such contrary evidence would be weighed against the evidence in support of its reliability to determine its ultimate reliability.

[
34
]

In
Borhot

voir dire
, I found the Crown had met the threshold for admissibility of the messages and posts. I also found the translations of the messages by Hanna and Cst El-Asmar were admissible as interpretive aids and were accurate and reliable. In assessing ultimate reliability, I adopt and rely on the evidence and reasoning set out in
Borhot

voir dire
in addition to the further evidence and considerations set out below.

[
35
]

There is no evidence in the trial proper that would raise a doubt about authentication, accuracy, or reliability of translations of the messages and posts. As such, for the same reasons outlined in
Borhot voir dire
, I find the posts and messages are reliable for the truth of their contents and admissible as party admissions against interest:
Evans

at p 664. I am equally satisfied the posts and messages were accurately and reliably translated. The posts and messages are now evidence to be weighed along with other circumstantial evidence to determine whether the Crown has proved the offences beyond a reasonable doubt.

[
36
]

At the conclusion of the trial, I considered all the evidence to determine the weight to give the messages and posts. There was little to no additional evidence to support the Defence’s assertion that the tendered posts and messages were not accurate and reliable recordings of the actual posts and messages. Other than disputing the affidavit of Cst Landon King, there was no evidence offered to suggest the Facebook raw data was inaccurate or the continuity compromised. Instead, two witnesses were questioned on whether portions of the record were an accurate representation of messages between those witnesses and the Accused. Both testified they would not have remembered the exchange without a printout of the conversation in front of them due to the passage of time. Neither of them testified the record or any part of it was a mischaracterization of the conversation, fictitious, made-up, or altered in any way. One witness inferred this by saying since the record was from the police, it “could” be an accurate recording. However, neither party questioned that witness further on that comment.

[
37
]

RCMP analyst Shawn Stewart testified he used a “translate” button to translate certain posts not written in English. Those particular posts were not translated by the translators and used Arabic characters and full sentences. The messages translated by the translators used an English keyboard to depict expressions, symbols, and other terms in Arabic, which may not as easily be translated. The Defence did not point out any inconsistencies, nor was there sufficient evidence offered to suggest the translations produced through the “translate” button were not accurate and reliable, although the evidence is less compelling than with the official translators.

b)

Authorship

[
38
]

Authorship can be inferred circumstantially though such things as the source of the information, access to the relevant social media address, disclosure of details known to the purported author, and the nature of the exchanges between the parties:
R v Durocher
,
2019 SKCA 97
[
Durocher
] at para
47
. It can also be inferred if the information in the posts and messages themselves reveals the purported author has knowledge that only the Accused would be likely to know:
Evans

at 663.

[
39
]

In
Borhot voir dire
, the Crown established on a balance of probabilities the Facebook Account belonged to the Accused and the Accused was the author of the posts and messages. The issue of authorship of the posts and messages was thoroughly considered (see paras 53-67). However, the Defence has raised issues that speak to the weight I can place on authorship of the posts and messages.

[
40
]

The Crown submits the Facebook Account contains a constellation of characteristics and facts sufficiently unique to the Accused and relies on their arguments and my findings in the
Borhot voir dire
. The Crown argues this is compelling circumstantial evidence the Accused controlled the Facebook Account at all material times and was the author of all posts and messages save for one: a message sent by the Accused’s mother from the Facebook Account.

[
41
]

The Crown submits the posts and messages originating from the Facebook Account were made by the Accused with this one exception. The Crown points to the content of the posts and messages themselves, the Accused’s admissions in interviews with the RCMP on May 22, 2014 and May 18, 2020, and evidence from Mohamad Chehade (Chehade) and Mohamad Samer Abdusallam (Abdusallam) to establish this fact.

[
42
]

The Defence argues the Crown has not proved beyond a reasonable doubt the Accused is the author of the posts and messages. The Defence argues there are many ways to make electronic evidence appear to be something other than what it is. The Court must be rigorous in its evaluation of the reliability and probative value of such evidence:
R v Aslami
,

2021 ONCA 249
[
Aslami
] at para
30
.
[1]

[
43
]

The Defence submits the posts and messages are unreliable. Only two of the eight individuals with whom the Accused communicated via the messages testified. The individuals involved in the remaining six conversations have not been affirmatively identified. The Defence notes the Court must consider the credibility of the witnesses purporting to authenticate authorship and any frailties in the evidence related to authorship. Specifically, the Defence submits the Court must consider whether:

•

the posts and messages reflect the whole truth;

•

other reasonable inferences from or about the posts are available;

•

the author is reliable; and

•

the relationship between the author and individuals to whom he is speaking is one that might lead to intimidation or lies, versus the truth.

[
44
]

Finally, the Defence submits the Accused lied to the RCMP during his interviews. Therefore, I should not rely on anything the Accused said to the RCMP.

[
45
]

During the Accused’s interviews with the RCMP on May 22, 2014 and May 18, 2020, the Accused admits the names jamal.borhot1, Muslim Borhot, and Muslim Khalafa are all names associated with his Facebook account. All three of those names were used for the Facebook Account. No rationale was provided for why the Accused would lie about this.

[
46
]

The Facebook Account’s “About” page contains photos of the Accused and information that the owner is from and lives in Calgary, attended the University of Calgary, and likes the video games “Battlefield” and “Call of Duty.” The author also likes and follows the FC Bayern München soccer team and follows the Calgary Stampeders football team. According to Chehade, FC Bayern München is the Accused’s favourite soccer team.

[
47
]

The content of the posts includes references to the city of Calgary and the author’s participation in events in Calgary. One post shared an article and petition on change.org about the approval of a land amendment application for an Islamic Centre located in Calgary. There are several posts about the Comic Expo in Calgary and the author’s participation at that event. The posts include a photo of the Accused with one of the celebrity delegates. There are several posts about the Calgary Flames hockey team including comments by the author in support of that team. The posts include many references to FC Bayern München soccer team. There are also posts about “Call of Duty” and “Battlefield,” which are listed as liked video games on the “About” page.

[
48
]

Frequent commentators on the posts include the usernames “Mohamad Bek Chehade”, “Samer M Abd”, and “Zeinab Borhot.” All three are included on the Facebook Account’s “Friends” page.

[
49
]

Chehade testified his Facebook username was “Mohamad Bek Chehade” and he was the author of comments and messages associated with that username that appeared on the Facebook Account. Abdusallam testified his Facebook username was “Samer M Abd” and he was the author of comments and messages associated with that username that appeared on the Facebook Account. Enga Deni testified Zeinab is the Accused’s mother. Posts and messages associated with the username “Zeinab Borhot” strongly infer the user is the Accused’s mother. The Accused does not dispute that fact.

Chehade

[
50
]

Chehade commented on many posts referencing FC Bayern München. In some of those posts, Chehade was tagged. The posts also include numerous references to the video games “Call of Duty” and “Battlefield,” including broadcasting the author’s game play. Chehade testified he played “Battlefield” online with the Accused.

[
51
]

Chehade testified he communicated with the Accused over Facebook before and after the Accused left Canada. He never thought the author of posts and messages from the Facebook Account was anyone other than the Accused. Chehade did not review all the Facebook materials given to him prior to testifying. He also had difficulty remembering the contents of the messages and assumed what the Crown gave him was accurate. However, he was confident the messages the Crown showed him were communications between him and the Accused. These frailties in his recollection and review of the messages limit the weight the court can place on his ability to confirm the accuracy of the content of the messages and his testimony in that respect. This limitation will be considered in light of other markers of reliability including how the source evidence was obtained (directly from FaceBook) and the other evidence adduced at trial.

[
52
]

Chehade testified he had a nickname the Accused used when the two of them spoke. The author of the messages frequently used that nickname. Chehade and the author of the messages talked about relevant things that Chehade and the Accused talked about. When the Crown asked Chehade if there was anything within the messages that would make him think it was not him and the Accused communicating, he said “On no, no. It’s definitely me” and the person he was communicating with was the Accused.

[
53
]

On August 19, 2013, Chehade sent a message to the Facebook Account asking, “is this jamal?” The author replies, “who else can that be brother...wow cubeyii have you forgotten me that quickly...may Allah forgive you.” Chehade testified he asked the question because the name on the Facebook Account had changed. However, Chehade knew he was communicating with the Accused during that conversation. He based this belief on the following:

•

He was sending messages to and receiving messages from the Facebook Account;

•

He had a nickname the Accused knew and was used by the author;

•

The two parties talked about things relevant to them both, including the last time Chehade saw the Accused before the Accused left Canada;

•

The author asked about common friends; and

•

Chehade’s history of conversations with the Facebook Account was consistent even when the name on the Facebook Account changed to “Muslim Khelafa.”

[
54
]

Chehade testified the “accent” used by the author in the messages between him and the Facebook Account changed partway through and the author used Turkish words. On April 3, 2014, Chehade sent a message stating: “now you talk with the dialect of Aleppo?” to which the author replied: “no I speak Lebanese.” The Defence argues this suggests there was tampering with the Facebook Account and raises a doubt about the Accused being the author of those particular messages. The Defence submits even if I am satisfied some of these messages were between the Accused and Chehade, there exists a doubt about whether all the messages sent from the Facebook Account were authored by the Accused. The Defence adduced no evidence of actual tampering of the Facebook Account.

[
55
]

The Defence argues Chehade’s evidence with respect to authorship should be given little weight. The Defence notes the history of messages between the Facebook Account and Chehade would have been available to anyone with access to the Facebook Account. Further, the Defence was prevented from cross-examining Chehade on issues that may have had relevance to authorship, including:

•

whether the witness had interactions with CSIS in general;

•

whether the witness had discussions with CSIS or a foreign government agency about the Accused in general and before they were interviewed by the RCMP;

•

whether CSIS or a foreign government agency told them information about the Accused’s travel outside Canada or affiliations with groups in Syria;

•

whether they asked the Accused questions on the request of CSIS or a foreign government agency;

•

whether they asked the Accused questions as a way to get information for CSIS or a foreign government agency;

•

whether CSIS or a foreign government agency gave them information to ask the Accused questions;

•

whether they received incentives (financial, immigration) from CSIS or a foreign government agency to report information about the Accused to those organizations or the RCMP;

•

whether they received promises of employment from any of those organizations;

•

whether they gave CSIS or a foreign government agency control over their Facebook account to engage with the Accused;

•

whether they obtained information from CSIS or a foreign government agency and claimed it as their own;

•

how believable the witness was due to his respective interests, associations, and sources of income;

•

whether the witness was receiving information from others that he used to entrap or threaten the Accused;

•

whether the Accused might have thought the witness was threatening him either physically or by virtue of his connections with others including law enforcement;

•

whether the Accused had reason to fear or lie to the witness;

•

whether the Accused had reason to think the witness was working for his mother and would alert her to bring him home from Turkey.

[
56
]

This list of questions come from Defence’s written submissions and requests at trial. At the end of Chehade’s examination, the Defence was given an opportunity to make submissions on any further questions he wanted to ask, including more generalized questions along some of the same topics. His only submission was he should have been able to ask the prohibited questions. Some of the Defence’s proposed questions involve asking Chehade to comment on what the Accused felt or thought. It was not privilege that prevented those questions from being asked, but general rules of evidence. A witnesses could not testify to what the Accused knew or how the Accused felt.

[
57
]

Chehade was called by the Crown primarily to prove the Accused was the author of the posts and messages. It is difficult to see how the questions proposed by the Defence would have had an impact on his evidence as it relates to authentication or authorship. Even if Chehade were instructed by CSIS to engage the Accused in conversation about his activities in Syria, he would have had to speak
with the Accused
about those things. The Defence was not barred from cross-examining Chehade about his memory of the messages or their interactions with the RCMP.

Abdusallam

[
58
]

Abdusallam testified he communicated directly with the Accused over Facebook, although he could not recall specifically what was communicated. In April 2014, the Accused came to stay with Abdusallam in Istanbul. A short time before then, Abdusallam sent the Accused a message that included Abdusallam’s phone number. He could not remember if that message was sent through Facebook. On March 28, 2014, the author of the Facebook Account sent a message to Abdusallam’s Facebook account seeking Abdusallam’s Turkish phone number. A phone number was provided in reply. Abdusallam did not contradict the accuracy of that phone number. I find this message was the message Abdusallam sent the Accused with his Turkish phone number.

[
59
]

Throughout the messages between Abdusallam and the Facebook Account, Abdusallam used the Accused’s first name, and the author used Abdusallam’s nickname that the Accused knew. The author also asked Abdusallam about school and the people in Canada, which were questions a stranger would be unlikely to know.

[
60
]

The Defence argues Abdusallam’s evidence about authorship should be given little weight. Abdusallam was unreliable with respect to authenticating the posts and messages. He testified he only recognized the conversations based on his name appearing in the record. Given the passage of time of 12 years since he had seen the messages, “there’s a chance that it is accurate.” Abdusallam also admitted his Facebook account had been hacked a few years prior to the conversations with the user of the Facebook Account. Further, like with Chehade, the Defence was prevented from cross-examining Abdusallam about similar topics, although the questions sought were more limited, and included questions pertaining to financial benefits, offers and incentives, including with respect to immigration and refugee status, offered in exchange for meeting with RCMP officers.

[
61
]

I accept the reliability of Abdusallam’s testimony in confirming the accuracy of the content of the messages is limited by his memory and the passage of time. The limitation in the weight that can be placed on this evidence will be considered in the context of the other markers of reliability and evidence adduced at trial. Like with the questions Defence was prevented from asking Chehade, Abdusallam could not testify as to what the Accused knew or how the Accused felt. Questions about entrapment would not speak to the issue of whether the messages were between Abdusallam and the Accused. The Defence argues someone other than the Accused posted the posts and messages on the Facebook Account without the Accused’s authorization. For example, there is evidence the Accused’s mother had access to the Facebook account and used it. The evidence available to suggest the posts and messages were authored by someone other than the Accused is limited to:

•

The IP addresses of the Facebook Account activity were not located in Syria;

•

The Accused’s mother was able to send a message from the Facebook Account to Chehade advising who she was and asking him to contact her urgently;

•

The Facebook Account’s password was changed on December 23, 2013;

•

Abdusallam testified in 2011 or 2012 someone hacked his own Facebook account and password in 2011 or which he noticed the same or next day;

•

There were long periods during which no posts or messages were being sent from the Facebook Account; and

•

A message from Chehade noting the Accused was “talking” with an Aleppo dialect.

[
62
]

The IP address information tendered does not appear to be an accurate reflection of where the Facebook Account activity actually originated. On March 13, 2013 such activity was identified as originating from IP addresses in Calgary. Between December 2013 and March 2014, such activity was identified as originating from IP addresses in Italy, London, and Iraq. There is no suggestion the Accused was in Italy, London, or Iraq during that time. From March 30 to April 18, 2014, such activity was identified as originating from IP addresses in Turkey. From April 19 to October 2016, such activity was identified as originating from IP addresses in Germany. After the Accused returned to Canada, the IP address continued to indicate activity on the Facebook Account originated in Germany.

[
63
]

On May 10, 2013, a message was sent from the Facebook Account to Chehade that states: “im jamals mother can u call plz at [number] urgent plz.” The Defence argues this shows the Accused did not have exclusive access to the Facebook Account and others were actively using the Facebook Account. The Defence further suggests a password change on December 23, 2013 indicates the possibility of a new user or an attempt to remove access from other users. The Defence draws this inference because password changes were “something not otherwise a matter of habit.”

[
64
]

The Crown concedes the message from May 10, 2013 suggests the Accused’s mother had access to the Facebook Account for a period of time. The Accused says so in certain messages. On March 27, 2013, in a conversation with “Mo Borhot,” Mo says “Listen, when you’re done, erase the chat lol. You mother is seeing them. The other day she saw me and told me haha.” The Accused responds “how did she see them... but I’ve changed the password.” And later “maybe at the time I hadn’t changed my password... now she can’t get in.” However, the Crown argues there is no other evidence of anyone other than the Accused’s mother using the Facebook Account. The Crown further submits there is no evidence with respect to how often the Facebook Account’s password was changed. As such, there is no evidence upon which to base the inference password changes were “something not otherwise a matter of habit” for the Accused.

[
65
]

Messages between the Facebook Account and other parties are contained in the messages tendered by the Crown. Those other parties did not testify at trial. Messages between “Zeinab Borhot” and the Facebook Account seem to be based on Zeinab’s belief that the author was her son. She used the Accused’s first name and asked whether the author was taking his medication, which is a notable personal detail. The author asked, “How is my dad?”, called Zeinab “mom” and “my beloved mother”, and referenced being detained by police in Germany. During the RCMP interviews, the Accused admitted he had been detained by police in Frankfurt, Germany.

[
66
]

Messages from “Mo Borhot” (Mo) and “Moe Borhot” (Moe) show circumstantial markers of familiarity. For example, throughout these conversations, the parties called each other cousin. Mo and Moe both used the Accused’s first name. Both conversations referred to people the two parties knew in common. Moe specifically referred to Hassan, the name of the Accused’s brother. In the communications with Moe, there are also references to playing “FIFA” and “Call of Duty,” which are video games Chehade testified he played with the Accused.

[
67
]

Messages from “Tarik Desouki” (Desouki) and “Ahmed Jadow” (Jadow) use the Accused’s first name. Desouki references playing “FIFA” and discusses people the two parties knew in common, including Hussain, which is the name of the person with whom the Accused is alleged to have left Canada. In the messages with Jadow, the author references being in Istanbul and waiting for a passport, and his family bringing him papers. During interviews with RCMP, the Accused described being in Istanbul, waiting for a passport after he had lost his, and his mother meeting him in Istanbul to bring him documents he needed to get a new passport.

[
68
]

There is nothing explicit in the communications with “Shahem Man” (Man) suggesting the Accused is the author of those messages, other than the fact the messages came from the Facebook Account, which is the same account from which the other messages originated.

[
69
]

The balance of the evidence refutes the Defence’s suggestion that someone other than the Accused gained control of the Facebook Account and made unauthorized posts and messages. The limited evidence in support of this argument is unpersuasive. Rather, throughout the various communications, the two participants discussed people in common and matters in which they shared an interest or memory. This is especially true with respect to messages with Chehade, including immediately prior to and after the message from the Accused’s mother, and when Chehade said the Accused was “talking” with an Aleppo dialect. There is no indication in the messages, nor did any witness testify to the Accused ever saying someone else got control of the Facebook Account and had posted or messaged in his stead, with one notable exception.

[
70
]

In April 2014, Chehade warned the Accused that police were asking questions about the Accused. The two discussed what the Accused would tell police, which included the Accused saying the Facebook Account was “penetrated” and the Syrian regime posted anything that might be incriminating. Chehade said he told police the Accused was in Syria to help the poor and needy and to volunteer for humanitarian help. This was the version of events the Accused told the RCMP after he returned to Canada.

[
71
]

I am satisfied the Crown has proved beyond a reasonable doubt the Accused is the owner of the Facebook Account and the author of the posts and messages. The cumulative effect of circumstantial evidence with respect to authorship when considered with the evidence as a whole allows me to draw that inference.

[
72
]

The URL itself is the Accused’s name. The Facebook Account is full of references to things that speak to the Accused’s personal circumstances, such as his social circle, individual preferences, and things the Accused either spoke about himself during his RCMP interviews or were testified about by other witnesses. The constellation of personal circumstances is sufficiently unique to the Accused to be probative. This is similar to the facts in
Evans

where a constellation of personal circumstances unique to that accused were used to describe the person to whom a witness sold the getaway car. The witness testified the buyer described himself as being employed as a chain-link fencer and owning a big dog that was having pups. Those personal circumstances matched those of Mr Evans. In light of this principle, I am satisfied the constellation of personal circumstances within the Facebook Account are sufficiently unique to infer the Accused is the owner of the Facebook Account and the author of the posts and messages.

[
73
]

I am also satisfied the Crown has proved the Accused to be the sending/replying party in the messages. The Accused admitted to RCMP that he used Facebook to communicate with his friends and family while he was travelling. There is also a significant amount of circumstantial evidence from within the messages themselves to infer the Accused is the author of the messages.

[
74
]

Looking at the body of messages as a whole, I find a strong inference that the Accused is the author of the messages with Chehede, Abdusallam, and Zeinab. I am satisfied the Facebook account with the username “Zeinab Borhot” belongs to the Accused’s mother. The account bears the name of the Accused’s mother. The content of the messages themselves strongly infers that to be the case. The evidence of the Accused as author of messages with the remaining people is not as strong as it is for Chehede, Abdusallam, and Zeinab. However, the inference that the Accused is the author of the messages with those three combined with the inference that the Facebook Account belongs to the Accused creates a strong inference that the Accused is also the author of the messages with Mo, Moe, Desouki, Jadow, and Man. Aside from messages with Man, which are neutral with respect to additional identifying features, the particular references within the conversations with Mo, Moe, Desouki, and Jadow also further strengthen that inference.

[
75
]

The inference that the Accused is the author of all posts and messages is further strengthened when looking at the Facebook evidence as a whole. When the inferences of authorship from the posts are combined with the constellation of personal circumstances, friends, and interests unique to the Accused and common in all the Facebook evidence, and pictures of the Accused, the inference that the Accused is the author of the posts is strong.

[
76
]

When looking at the evidence as a whole, the inference that the Accused is the owner of the Facebook Account and the author of the posts and messages is even stronger. The Accused made several admissions in his RCMP interviews about his Facebook Account that corroborate the information contained in the Facebook Account. Further, the descriptions Chehade and Abdusallam gave about their electronic conversations with the Accused are also consistent with those conversations having occurred via the Facebook Account.

[
77
]

Even if I accept the Defence’s arguments about innocent explanations for some individual pieces of evidence, my conclusions about authorship of the posts and messages remains the same. Other arguments of the Defence are harder to accept without any evidence in support. These include Defence’s arguments that the Accused was lying to the RCMP when he said the Facebook Account was his, and details the Accused confirmed during the RCMP interviews that are corroborative of what was contained in the Facebook messages. Examined separately and in isolation, some of these individual pieces of evidence
may
create a doubt. But the individual pieces of evidence must be considered in relation to the whole. It is the whole of the evidence taken together whose cumulative force must be considered as a basis for a finding of guilt. When I examine the evidence as a whole, there is no other reasonable inference to be drawn other than the Accused is both the owner of the Facebook Account and the author of the posts and messages.

]

I am satisfied the Crown has proved beyond a reasonable doubt the voice identified as the Accused in the wiretap recordings and transcripts is that of the Accused. The cumulative effect of circumstantial evidence with respect to voice identification when considered with the evidence as a whole supports that finding. [

]

I am satisfied Csts Khalil and Checkley accurately identified the voice of the Accused from the recordings that were put to them. I put significant weight on their evidence on this point. Not every single wiretap recording upon which the Crown relies was put to them. However, it was not necessary to do so. There was no evidence to suggest the voice the officers identified as the Accused was not that of the Accused. Both officers had significant exposure to the Accused’s voice. Both saw and heard the Accused speak during the Accused’s RCMP interviews. Cst Checkley watched and listened to those interviews. Cst Khalil personally participated in one such interview. Both officers also spent several hours listening to wiretap recordings to the point that the voices heard on the recordings became familiar to them. While Cst Checkley found it easier to identify the Accused’s voice when he was speaking English, Cst Khalil understood Arabic and identified the Accused speaking in both Arabic and English. Both officers identified specific features of the Accused’s voice that was different than the other voices heard on the wiretap recordings.

[
115
]

I am also able to do my own comparison between recordings that are known to be the Accused’s voice and the wiretap recordings. I have watched and listened to the Accused’s RCMP interviews. There are instances in the wiretap recordings where the Accused self-identifies. Using those audio examples, I can identify the distinct tone of the Accused’s voice in the other wiretap recordings. Within the wiretap recordings themselves, other speakers identify the Accused, which is circumstantial evidence from which an inference can be drawn that the Accused is one of the other speakers. The circumstantial evidence from the surveillance witnesses also strengthens that inference.

[
116

PROOF OF ESSENTIAL ELEMENTS

1)

The Law

[
164
]

Section 83.18(1)
of the
Criminal Code
states:

Every one who knowingly participates in or contributes to any activity of a terrorist group for the purpose of enhancing the ability of any terrorist group to facilitate or carry out a terrorist activity is guilty of an indictable offence and liable to imprisonment for a term not exceeding 10 years.

[
165
]

The Crown must prove beyond a reasonable doubt:

(e)

The Accused knowingly participated in or contributed to (directly or indirectly) an activity of a terrorist group; and

(f)

The Accused’s actions were undertaken for the purpose of enhancing the abilities of a terrorist group to facilitate or carry out terrorist activity.

[
166
]

Different iterations of the applicable test have been cited in Canadian case law. The Court in
R v NY
,
2008 CanLII 24543 (ON SC)
paras
7-10
, laid out a framework for the elements of the offence based on the analysis in
R v Khawaja
,
2008 CanLII 92005 (ON SC)
:

(a)

A terrorist group existed;

(b)

The accused knew of the existence of the terrorist group;

(c)

The accused participated in or contributed to, directly or indirectly, any activity of the terrorist group; and

(d)

The participation or contribution was intended by the accused to enhance the ability of a terrorist group to facilitate or carry out a terrorist activity.

R v NY,
2008 CanLII 51935
at para
154
;
R v Hersi,
2014 ONSC 1217
at para
13
;
R v Hersi,
2014 ONSC 2894 at para 12
;
R v Ansari,
2015 ONCA 575
at para
165
.

Terrorist Group

[
167
]

Breaking these elements down further, the Crown must prove a terrorist group existed. This is met when the Crown proves the group is an entity (a person, group, trust, partnership, fund, or unincorporated association or organization that is distinct from the Accused) whose purpose or activities is the facilitation or carrying out of terrorist activity
or
is a listed entity on the Governor-in-Council’s list.

[
168
]

The Defence suggests the Governor-in-Council’s list merely serves as a form of public notice that a listed entity is treated as a terrorist group under Canadian law. Before an entity is listed, it cannot be assumed that individuals will have knowledge the entity is considered a terrorist group under Canadian law. The Crown must therefore prove beyond a reasonable doubt it would be reasonable for the Accused to know a group with which they were dealing is an entity engaged in terrorist activity. Further, the Defence argues since the Governor-in-Council’s list allows a group to be listed as a terrorist group on reasonable grounds to believe it is such, the Crown cannot rely on the listing alone to prove a terrorist group beyond a reasonable doubt. After an entity is listed by the Governor-in-Council, the Crown is therefore required to prove the listing is justified on a beyond a reasonable doubt standard. The Crown may not back-date the status of an entity that becomes a terrorist group to before it began carrying out terrorist activity. Entities must be analyzed as they were acting and known by the Accused to act at the time of the Accused’s participation. In other words, the Crown must prove beyond a reasonable doubt an entity’s prior terrorist activity and that such activity was known to the Accused before the alleged participation by the Accused.

[
169
]

I agree with the Defence that the activities of the group cannot be back-dated as a terrorist group to before it began carrying out terrorist activities or the list-designation back-dated to before the group was listed on the Governor-in-Council list. If the group’s status is unclear at the time the Accused is alleged to have left Canada and remained in Syria, it is to the Accused’s benefit. I agree the Crown must prove beyond a reasonable doubt the entity was a terrorist organization at the time the alleged offences were committed and the Accused knew them to be such an organization at the relevant time. Regarding entities on the Governor-in-Counsel list, I disagree with Defence that the Crown must separately prove: 1) an entity on the list was in fact a terrorist organization based on its prior terrorist activity, and 2) the listing as a terrorist group is justified on a beyond a reasonable doubt standard. To require this is to render the Governor-in-Council’s list nugatory and ignore the specific wording of the legislation.

Terrorist Activity

[
170
]

“Terrorist activity” is defined through a conduct component and a mental component. The conduct component

is proven by:

(e)

An enumerated consequence listed in
Criminal Code

s 83.01, defined as an act or omission that actually causes death, serious bodily harm, endangerment to life, risk to public health and safety, substantial property damage, or serious interference with an essential service or facility:
Criminal Code
s 83.01 “terrorist activity” s (b)(ii)(A-E); or

(f)

A conspiracy, attempt, threat, or counselling to commit an act or omission that, if performed, would likely lead to one of the enumerated consequences:
Criminal Code

s 83.01 “terrorist activity: s (b)(ii)(E); or

(g)

Acting as an accessory after the fact to an act or omission that led to one of the enumerated consequences:
Criminal Code

s 83.01 “terrorist activity: s (b)(ii)(E).

[
171
]

The definition of “terrorist activity” excludes acts or omissions committed during certain forms of armed conflict or the activities undertaken by military forces of a state in the exercise of their official duties under certain circumstances.

[
172
]

The mental component

of a terrorist activity is proven when the following three elements are present:

(h)

Intention: the terrorist activity must be done with the intention of causing one of the enumerated consequences listed in
Criminal Code

s 83.01;

(i)

Ulterior intention: the terrorist activity must be done with the further intention of either intimidating the public with regards to its safety, or compelling a person, government, or organization to either do or not do something; and

(j)

Motive: the terrorist activity must be done for a religious, political, or ideological purpose, objective, or cause.

Criminal Code

s 83.01 “terrorist activity”: (b)(i)(A-B);
R v Khawaja
,
2010 ONCA 862
[
Khawaja ONCA
] at paras
82-85
.

Knowledge of the Accused

[
173
]

If the Crown proves a terrorist group existed, the Accused must subjectively know or be wilfully blind to the circumstances that render the entity a “terrorist group,” such as the nature of the terrorist group’s activities generally. The Accused must also know that the thing in which he is participating or contributing is "an activity" of that group (not necessarily a terrorist activity). There is no requirement that the Accused know specifics of the terrorist group’s activities:
R v Nadarajah
,
2010 ONCA 859
[
Nadarajah
] at para
22
. The Court may look at expert evidence on the predominate thrust of the group’s activities and evidence of the Accused’s own interests and intentions:
R v Hersi
,
2014 ONSC 2897
[
Hersi #1
] at para
20
.

Participation or Contribution

[
174
]

If the Crown proves the Accused knew or was wilfully blind to the existence of the terrorist group, the Crown must then prove the Accused participated in, or contributed to, directly or indirectly, any activity of the terrorist group beyond
de minimis
. This is met if the Crown proves the Accused’s acts were associated with
any
activity of the terrorist group (not just terrorist activity) if that activity enhances the terrorist group’s ability to engage in terrorist activity:
Nadarajah

at para
20
. This can be proved with evidence including that the Accused:

•

Provided, received, or recruited a person to receive training;

•

Provided or offered skills or expertise for the benefit of, at the direction of or in association with a terrorist group;

•

Recruited a person to facilitate or commit an act in or outside Canada that would be a terrorism offence if committed in Canada;

•

Entered or remained in a country for the benefit of, at the direction of, or in association with a terrorist group;

•

Made himself available to facilitate or commit an act in or outside Canada that would be a terrorism offence if committed in Canada, in response to instructions from any of the persons who constitute a terrorist group.

Criminal Code

s 83.18(3)

[
175
]

Examples of things that constitute evidence of the Accused’s participation or contribution include:

•

Use of names, words, symbols, or other representations that are associated with the terrorist group;

•

Frequent association with members of the terrorist group;

•

Receiving any benefit from the terrorist group;

•

Repeated engagement in activities at the instruction of members of the terrorist group.

Criminal Code

s 83.14(4)

[
176
]

Neither of these lists are exhaustive. The ordinary meaning of “participation” and “contribution” still applies, which means that other factual scenarios could yield other ways of participating or contributing to the activities of a terrorist group:
Nadarajah
at paras
18-19
. The Crown does not need to prove the Accused’s acts actually enhanced the terrorist group’s ability to carry out terrorist activity:
R v Khawaja
,
2012 SCC 69
[
Khawaja SCC
] at para
41
. However, the Crown does need to prove the Accused’s acts contributed more than a negligible risk to society or the Accused’s conduct was
capable
of materially helping the terrorist group’s ability to exercise its core terrorist function. In other words, the Accused’s actions must exceed the
de minimis
threshold:
Khawaja SCC
at paras
49-51
. Innocent or socially useful conduct undertaken absent any intent to enhance or conduct a reasonable person would not view as capable of materially enhancing the ability of a terrorist group to facilitate or carry out terrorist activity falls below the
de minimis
threshold:
Khawaja SCC

at para
53
.

[

at para

Nadarajah

at para

Nadarajah

at para
25
. The Accused’s knowledge and intentions are likely not directly provable; they can be discerned from the Accused’s actions and words and inferred from other facts, in light of common sense and logic:

,
2008 CanLII 92005
(ONSC) at paras
94-95

A)

Particularization

[

Count 1 requires the Crown to prove the Accused left Canada or entered Syria for the purpose of engaging in activities that would enhance a terrorist group in carrying out terrorist activities. No terrorist group is particularized. The Crown must therefore prove the Accused had the intention, at a point in the future, to engage in such activities for one or more terrorist groups. If the Crown proves the Accused, when leaving Canada or entering Syria, had the desire to join one or more terrorist groups with knowledge of those terrorist group’s purposes, the
mens rea
for this offence will be met:
R v Hersi
,
2014 ONSC 4143
[
Hersi #2
] at para
19
. Circumstantial evidence of the Accused’s intention upon leaving Canada or entering Syria may be found in evidence of the Accused’s beliefs and activities before he left Canada:
Hersi #2

at para
39
. An inference may be drawn that the Accused’s act of boarding a flight leaving Canada was the first step in the implementation of a plan to join a terrorist group in Syria. This inference may be drawn even if multiple steps would need to be taken before the crime is completed or if the plan was ultimately not accomplished:
Hersi #2
at paras
29-30
.

[
179
]

Count 2 requires the Crown to prove the Accused remained in Syria for the benefit of, at the direction of, or in association with the Islamic State. There is no case law that interprets these requirements. This offence criminalizes the Accused’s actions of remaining in Syria to further the activities of the Islamic State. Remaining in Syria in and of itself is an innocuous act. As such, the Crown must prove the Accused’s intention in remaining in Syria was to further the activities of the Islamic State. The Crown does not need to prove such an intention crystalized at a specific point in time. The offence is one of continuous conduct. As such, the Crown need only prove the Accused remained in Syria with such an intention at some point during the specified timeframe in order to make out the offence. If the Crown proves the Accused formed such an intention while he was in Syria, the offence would continue unless and until the Accused abandoned that intention or left Syria.

[
180
]

Count 3 particularises the Islamic State as the terrorist group for whom the Accused knowingly participated in or contributed to activities. Count 3 also particularises the activities in which the Accused participated included one or more terrorist acts. The Crown must therefore prove at some point during the specified timeframe, the Accused’s activities were intentionally directed towards enhancing the activities of the Islamic State and those activities included on at least one occasion a terrorist act.

B)

Analysis

A)

Terrorist Group

[
181
]

The Crown has identified three entities as terrorist groups for the purpose of Count 1: al Nusra, al-Qaeda, and the Islamic State. The Crown argues the Accused left Canada and entered Syria with the intention of joining one of these three groups. I am satisfied the Crown has proved beyond a reasonable doubt that all three entities were terrorist groups at the time of the offences.

[
182
]

For the relevant period for Count 1, Al-Qaeda and the Islamic State were listed entities on the Governor-in-Counsel’s list. Al Nusra was not a listed entity in Canada until November 2013. For the relevant period for Counts 2 and 3, Al-Qaeda and the Islamic State were listed entities, and al Nusra was a listed entity for a portion of the relevant period. As such, they meet the second definition of “terrorist group” in
Criminal Code

s 83.01(1).

[
183
]

Alternatively, I am satisfied at the relevant time, all three groups had as one or more of its purposes or activities facilitating or carrying out terrorist activities, meeting the first definition of “terrorist group.”

(A)

Al-Qaeda

[
184
]

Dr Steinberg testified al-Qaeda is a Sunni Muslim organization that believes in establishing Islamic or Shari’ah law. It uses instability in countries like Syria, Iraq, and Afghanistan to immerse itself into insurgencies to advance its goal. Since inception, al-Qaeda had as its aims to topple authoritarian regimes in Egypt, Saudi Arabia, and other countries. Al-Qaeda was responsible for toppling the Twin Towers in New York City on September 11, 2001 and engaged in attacks on politicians, religious leaders, and civilians in several countries. Al-Qaeda seeks allegiances and builds good relations with other insurgent organizations to reach its aims. Al-Qaeda was established and active during the relevant time period.

[
185
]

It is clear from Dr Steinberg’s evidence that, at the time of the offences, al-Qaeda engaged in terrorist activity. At the time of the offences, it was engaging in acts for political, religious, and ideological objectives. It used extreme acts of violence to intimidate or compel certain governments to withdraw so it could establish a Shari’ah state. It caused substantial property damage and loss of life through its acts.

(B)

The Islamic State

[
186
]

Dr Steinberg testified the Islamic State first emerged in Iraq in 2000 in close cooperation with al-Qaeda. Like al-Qaeda, the Islamic State is a Sunni Muslim organization whose goal is to introduce and establish Islamic or Shari’ah law. It rejects all other Muslim sects and believe any non-Sunni are unbelievers and not Muslims at all. It does not cooperate with other Muslim groups and treat Shia Muslims with particular brutality. The Islamic State extolls that every true Sunni Muslim has a right to join the Islamic State, which means the Islamic State has and will accept any Sunni Muslim who pledges allegiance to it. However, any person who does not convert to Sunni Islam and pledge allegiance to the Islamic State will be killed. The Islamic State does not believe in alliances and does not cooperate with other insurgent organizations. The Islamic State was established and active during the relevant time periods.

[
187
]

Dr Steinberg testified the Islamic State is a Salafist organization. There are many Salafists, some of whom are predominantly peaceful. Salafists believe in order to reform Islam and the Muslim world, they must return to the sources and rebuild society along the lines of early Islam. However, the Islamic State is a Salafi-Jihadi organization. Its members believe, in order to rebuild societies in the Muslim world, they have to fight in a holy war called Jihad, which means to fight against the enemies of Islam. In their fighting practices, they return to early Islamic ways but with modern weaponry.

[
188
]

Dr Amarsignam also testified the Islamic State is a Salafist-Jihadi organization. In Syria, it was interested in ousting the al-Assad Regime. However, its main goal was to create an Islamic State in Syria. Jihadists want an Islamic State or Caliphate. This is distinct from Salafists, who are conservative Islamists. The classification of a group as a Salafist-Jihadi organization was not necessarily synonymous with an understanding that the group was also a terrorist group. However, the Islamic State is a violent extremist Salafist-Jihadi organization. Its members do not believe in engaging in the political process. They believe democracy is polytheistic or spiritually corrupt.

[
189
]

It is clear from the evidence of both Dr Steinberg and Dr Amarsignam that the Islamic State engaged in terrorist activity at the time of the offences. At the time of the offences, it was engaging in acts for political, religious, and ideological objectives. It used extreme acts of violence to intimidate or compel governments to withdraw so they could establish a Shari’ah state. It engaged in particularly brutal acts of violence against a specific Muslim sect. It caused substantial property damage and loss of life through its acts.

(C)

Jabhat al-Nusra

[

]

Dr Amarsignam testified, like the Islamic State, al Nusra is a Salafist-Jihadi organization whose main goal was to create an Islamic State or Caliphate in Syria. Al Nusra had been a well-known Jihadist group in Syria for some time. It was listed by the United States and the United Nations as a terrorist group in December 2012 and by Canada in November 2013. At that time, the designation of al Nusra as a terrorist group was treated with scepticism and pushback by regular civilians in Syria as an attempt to interfere with the revolution. Some opined the designation was inappropriate.

[

]

While it was not a listed entity on the Governor-in-Counsel’s list when the Accused left Canada, it was listed as a terrorist group in the United States. By 2006, there was a substantial foreign fighter presence in Iraq, mainly in the ranks of the Islamic State. The leader of al Nusra refused to accept the Islamic State in Iraq’s declaration and claimed both organizations were part of al-Qaeda, to whom its allegiance was pledged in 2004. 1)

Expert Evidence

[

]

Dr Amarsignam testified by August 2011, Syria’s civil war against the al-Assad Regime was in full force. Small groups of civilians worked under larger umbrella organizations to oppose the al-Assad Regime. Some of the groups in Syria at that time were solely interested in the removal of al-Assad. Groups united for the sole purpose of fighting against the al-Assad Regime even though they did not share ideologies. Movement between fighting groups was fairly fluid. A large number of foreign fighters went to Syria.

[
208
]

Dr Amarsignam testified in 2012 and 2013, the Islamic State and al Nusra accepted foreign fighters, including those from the West. Other groups did not tend to accept foreign fighters, especially those from the West. However, there was a reluctance to bring in Western foreign fighters for fear that they may be American plants. Al Nusra did not accept just anyone. A
tazkiya
or vouching system was used for new arrivals. In the early stages there was a concern that integrating someone who did not speak Arabic would be difficult. Unless a person had such a
tazkiya
, it would have been difficult to join al Nusra.

[
209
]

At the Kilis border crossing between Turkey and Syria, a
tazkiya
was not necessary. A person who knew someone in Syria might have still used a smuggler or fixer to enter Syria. It was also not necessary to have prior communication with the group the person intended to join. Sometimes the decision to join a group was based on who controlled the border area where the person crossed or the first group the person encountered upon crossing. It would be difficult, however, to determine which group a person joined based solely on the point of entry. The process of going to training camps for firearms training was basically the same between different organizations.

[
210
]

Dr Steinberg explained in early 2013, many fighters joined the Islamic State. The numbers grew because of individuals or small groups changing affiliation or wholesale absorption of groups by the Islamic State. 4)

Conclusions

[
248
]

The Crown has proved beyond a reasonable doubt the Accused participated in or contributed to activities of the Islamic State. When the Accused’s communications and conversations are put into context with the expert evidence, I am satisfied the only reasonable inference that can be drawn is the Accused knew he was part of a terrorist organization, understood their goals of achieving a Caliphate State through Jihad, and participated in their activities in achieving that goal by committing acts of violence. As such, the Crown has proved beyond a reasonable doubt the Accused intended to enhance the ability of the Islamic State to facilitate or carry out terrorist activities in Syria and the Accused committed terrorist acts at the direction of or in association with the Islamic State.

VII.

Conclusion

[
249
]

The Crown has proved beyond a reasonable doubt the elements of all three offences.

[
250
]

The Crown has proved beyond a reasonable doubt the following:

•

Al Qaeda, al Nusra, and the Islamic State were terrorist groups engaging in terrorist activities at the relevant time (Counts 1-3);

•

The acts committed by al Nusra and the Islamic State were done with the intent to cause one or more of the enumerated consequences listed in
Criminal Code

s 83.01. These include an act or omission that actually causes death, serious bodily harm, endangerment to life, risk to public health and safety, substantial property damage, or serious interference with an essential service or facility. Those activities were done with the further intention of either intimidating the public with regards to its safety, or compelling a person, government, or organization (including the al-Assad government) to either do or not do something. There was a clear religious, political, or ideological purpose, objective, or cause to the commission of these terrorist acts. The Accused intended to enhance the ability of al Nusra and Islamic State respectively to facilitate or carry out these activities (Counts 1-3)
.

•

The Accused knew or was wilfully blind that the Islamic State was a terrorist group. He knew the Islamic State’s goal of toppling the al-Assad government through violence and replacing it with a Salafist government and creating an Islamic State or Caliphate in Syria. While in Syria, he was aware of activities of the Islamic State which meet the definition of “terrorist activities”. While the Accused may not have believed al Nusra was a terrorist group, prior to departing Canada and while in Syria, he knew of its activities, and those activities meet the definition of “terrorist activities”. He either subjectively knew or was wilfully blind to the circumstances that rendered al Nusra a “terrorist group”. (Counts 1-3);

•

The Accused held extremist beliefs consistent with the goals of both al Nusra and the Islamic State of creating a Caliphate State through violence. He made it clear he wanted to extend that Caliphate beyond the borders of Syria and he was prepared to both kill and die for his beliefs (Counts 1-3);

•

The Accused left Canada and entered Syria with the intention of joining a terrorist group and participating in activities that would enhance that group’s goals. Based on the posts made before the Accused left Canada, I am satisfied the Accused intended to join al Nusra when he arrived in Syria, knowing or being willfully blind to the fact that al Nusra was a terrorist group. In the alternative, he left with the intent to join the Islamic State, knowing the Islamic State was a terrorist group (Count 1);

•

The Accused remained in Syria for the benefit of the Islamic State. He used firearms with the intention of killing anyone who was non-Muslim. He intended those violent acts to aid the Islamic State in achieving their goals. These are terrorist activities. He often used terms such as “us” and “we” when referring to violent acts against non-Muslims, Shiites, and the al-Assad Regime (Count 2);

•

The Accused participated in activities of the Islamic State for the purpose of supporting them in achieving their goals. He was in management and ranked an officer for the Islamic State. He created videos at the direction of and for the benefit of the Islamic State. He attempted to recruit several others to join him in Syria and engage in Jihad for the benefit of the Islamic State. These constitute terrorist activities (Count 3); and

•

Activities of the Islamic State caused serious risk to the health or safety of the public and caused substantial property damage with the intention of toppling the al-Assad Regime and replacing it with a Salafist government. The Islamic State’s ultimate goal was to rid Syria of any “non-believers” of the Salafist movement to create an Islamic State or Caliphate in Syria through slaughter. The Accused participated in those activities with the intention of enhancing the Islamic State’s ability to achieve their goal and to rid Syria of any non-Muslim believers (Counts 1-3).

[
251
]

I am satisfied the only reasonable inference to be drawn from the evidence is that the Accused is guilty of all three offences.
